title: This Beetle Fires Boiling Spray 500 Times a Second
subject: bombardier beetle

scenes.text: This beetle fires boiling poison from its rear. How does its own body survive?
The bombardier beetle. Its spray hits about 100 degrees Celsius, the boiling point of water.
It doesn't fire a stream. It fires roughly 500 tiny pulses every second, at up to 22 miles an hour.
Two chemicals, hydrogen peroxide and hydroquinones, sit apart inside it. Enzymes mix them into a violent reaction.
The reaction happens in a small chamber, one droplet at a time. The pulses give it a chance to cool between shots.
It even aims, using plates on its abdomen. Boiling, in pulses. That's how a beetle survives its own explosion.

description:
The bombardier beetle fires a spray at about 100 degrees Celsius, in roughly 500 pulses a second.
Hydrogen peroxide and hydroquinones are stored apart, then mixed by enzymes in a small reaction chamber. Firing in pulses lets the chamber cool between shots, and reflector plates on the abdomen help it aim.

first_comment: Which would you rather meet: a bombardier beetle or a pistol shrimp? Both fire at things with chemistry and physics we barely match.
